note: What the switch-level run in netlist.py reads, so a copy you already own can be confirmed before it is trusted. Nothing here is any part of the files: a digest identifies one, and no set of digests reconstructs anything.
why: This is a netlist extracted from die photographs of a real part, so it answers questions no document and no recording can: what is inside the package. It is somebody else's work, so what is carried is the identity and the program that reads it.
whyRungThree: Independent research. Below the manufacturer's own documents and below a recording taken off a real part, because a netlist is an extraction and an extraction can be wrong. Nothing in this package is held to it; it is used to ask questions, and an answer it gives is recorded as coming from it.
obtaining: The three files are in chip-z80 in the Visual 6502 repository. Clone it, or take the three named files from it, and put them in docs/independent/visual6502. The digests below decide whether what arrived is what was read.
licence: The Visual 6502 repository states that licences and copyright are per file. The three files here carry no header of their own. They are read and never redistributed by this project, which is why nothing is carried.

algorithm.note: The resolver in netlist.py follows chipsim.js and wires.js from the same repository, which do carry a licence.

decides: sha256 decides. crc32 is published beside it so a copy can be cross-checked against a catalogue that keys on it, and it decides nothing on its own: it is a 32-bit error code.

files.what: Every named net, including vss, vcc and clk, whose numbers 1, 2 and 3 every rule in netlist.py is written against.
The polygons, read here only for the one column that marks a net as permanently pulled up.
Every transistor: its gate and its two channel connections. The circuit itself.
